  become increasingly popular in various settings, including smart homes and
  public transportation systems. Fingerprinting-based localization technology
  has gained significant attention due to its high accuracy and relatively simple
  implementation. However, it generates substantial power consumption and data
  traffic costs due to the necessity to collect and update location databases
  frequently. In contrast, decentralized algorithms for localization have lower
  operational expenses but often compromise on positioning accuracy. To address
  this issue, we present a novel algorithm called Decentralized Discriminative

  a promising technology that detects respiratory issues by analyzing sounds from 
  the lungs. However, the complexity of lung sounds poses a challenge for 
  automated analysis, with the need for a reliable method to identify the optimal 
  analysis window size to accurately detect pathological features and conditions. 
  Until now, window sizes have been chosen arbitrarily or based on breathing 
  rate, without considering the physiological basis of lung sounds. Our research 
  presents a novel approach to determine the optimal analysis window size for 
  acoustic lung data classification using exponential decay modeling. We tested this 
  approach on two distinct datasets, with results showing that a fixed window 
  size of 0.625 seconds yields the highest classification accuracy across all breathing 
  rates for both datasets. This finding is particularly significant, as it implies 
  that a universally applicable analysis window size exists, which can be used 
  for the analysis of lung sounds across various subjects, breathing rates, and 
  conditions without the need for further adjustments. Ultimately, our discovery 
  offers a practical solution to simplify the analysis of lung sounds, paving the 
  way for more accessible and user-friendly at-home monitoring devices. Our code

  remains poorly understood. To address this, we analyzed 24 years of data from the

  behavior of 136 non-active galaxies in the central region of the Milky Way. Our
  findings reveal that the optical and UV luminosities of these galaxies follow a
  consistent pattern of increase during the winter months and decrease during the
  summer months. This seasonal pattern is not attributed to changes in the

  of galaxies on the color-mass diagram. Instead, we propose that the optical and
  UV variability is primarily influenced by the interaction between the galaxies

  the galaxy is surrounded by a diffuse gas that enhances their luminosity.  To
  account for the variability in the UV spectrum, specifically the rise in the

  from a reservoir of low-metallicity gas that is more prominent during this time
  period. This is supported by the similar variability exhibited by the central
  supermassive black hole at the galaxy's core, Sgr A*.  We propose that this gas
  is linked to the galactic wind that the galaxy experiences during the approach
  to the perihelion, and which leads to the formation of a circumgalactic medium

  spectra of the galaxies and Sgr A*.  We also found that the interaction with
  this gas results in the emission of the MIR nuclear radiation that has been
  observed in some of these galaxies.  This research highlights the significance
  of considering the interaction between the galaxies and their surroundings during

We introduce a new approach to tackle this issue using multi-agent systems, specifically designing an optimization problem that co-authors can solve independently to achieve a mutually beneficial outcome. This optimization problem is addressed using an innovative application of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm, which we adapt to handle large-scale data and soft-constraints. We tested this approach on a large, real-world dataset and the results showed significant improvements in co-author suggestions. This achievement led to the development of a robust predictive model, which in turn enabled us to create a co-author recommendation system. This system was successfully integrated into our research paper writing platform, providing valuable suggestions to users based on both their past collaborations and the content of their papers. This platform has been in use for over a year at our institution, with over 200 users and more than 500 research papers listed on it. This platform's success serves as a solid foundation for further expansion, including the integration of additional data sources and machine learning components to enhance its collaboration suggestion features. This platform is open to public use under the Apache 2.0 license and its source code is available on GitHub. (OOD) user-generated content on social media platforms is critical to ensure the effectiveness and safety of these platforms.  As a result, developing accurate and robust methods for detecting OOD content is essential.  Since annotated data sets for this specific task are scarce and expensive to obtain, it is vital to explore alternative training data that is readily available but may not be directly relevant.  This research focuses on leveraging pre-trained language models for transfer learning to detect OOD content.  In this context, we investigate the use of text classification tasks with large datasets that differ from the target task in terms of distribution.  To evaluate the robustness of our method, we conducted multiple experiments using the SNLI and CommonsenseQA datasets that have OOD characteristics.  Our results show that these datasets, although not directly related to the target task, can serve as effective training data.  Furthermore, we discovered that fine-tuning the model on the minority class of the SNLI dataset enhances its ability to detect OOD content.  Finally, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive Threshold Transfer (ATT) that adapts the threshold used for classification based on the specific characteristics of the transfer data.  Our ATT method outperforms the baseline on the test set, achieving an F1-score of 0.93 on the Reddit dataset.  Our research provides a foundation for exploring alternative training data that can enhance the performance of OOD text classification tasks.  To facilitate further research, we made our code and model available for public access.  Our research also highlights the potential of fine-tuning on minority classes and introduces the ATT method as a novel approach for adapting classification thresholds in transfer learning.  Our findings on the benefits of fine-tuning on minority classes and the ATT method are significant discoveries that can be applied to related natural language processing tasks.   of dark matter annihilation, with various properties, on the large-scale

  (6.9 to 15) and on galaxy groups with exceptionally high masses (10 to the

  in order to leave a detectable imprint on galaxy groups at those times.

  suggests that alternative explanations for potential group mass dependencies

observed phenomenon, and it leads to particles settling into a stable state

indicates the variety of particles at each network node. Our findings show that 
there are two main network node types: those with a steady state that's a 
constant, and those with a state that changes in response to changes in the 
network. We've created a new measure, 'good mixability,' specifically to 
characterize the latter type of nodes. Our research demonstrates that network 
nodes with good mixability can be accurately described using a simple, two-part 
formula, and this formula has a clear and direct relationship with another 
measure, 'algebraic distance.' We've also discovered that network nodes with 
good mixability have unique'memory,' and this memory is directly linked to 
their geometric structure. Furthermore, we've developed a new method to assess 
the mixability of network nodes in a general, algorithmic way, and this method 
is based on solving a system of polynomial equations. We've applied our research 
to investigate a specific problem related to the spread of 'defective' particles 
in networks, and our findings show that optimizing network node diversity can 
significantly improve the spread of 'healthy' particles. We've also introduced 
a new, random network algorithm that generates networks with unique, geometric 
properties, and this algorithm is a generalization of an existing algorithm.

patterns, and it provides a practical application for future research related 
to particle transportation in networks. We've validated our algorithm by 
conducting simulations and comparing the results with theoretical predictions, 
and our findings show that the algorithm generates networks that conform to 
specific, predictable patterns. We've also applied our algorithm to simulate 
real-world network scenarios, and this includes networks with unique'memory' 
patterns that are influenced by geographical features, such as mountains 
ranges. We believe that our algorithm and the associated research provide a 
useful foundation for future studies related to particle transportation in 
networks. We've made our algorithm publicly available, and it can be used by

training large models on a vast amount of data remains computationally expensive due to memory constraints. Interpreting model performance as an optimization process, where the model's fitness is evaluated against its own fitness landscape, can provide valuable insights into its behavior. In this research, training a ResNet-50 model on ImageNet data is examined as an optimization process where the model's fitness is assessed against its own landscape, revealing an irregular search space with inconsistent local optima, slow movement in the early stages of training, and a sudden shift in the latter stages. This irregularity is attributed to the conflicting requirements of image classification and the need for generalization, resulting in performance that is both unstable and unpredictable in the initial stages of training. Furthermore, the non-uniformity of the fitness landscape is demonstrated by the varying smoothness of local areas, and the presence of multiple, distinct, and long-lasting plateaus is observed, posing challenges for optimization algorithms. This analysis highlights the complexity of the fitness landscape in deep learning and the limitations of optimization algorithms, offering a foundation for exploring more effective optimization methods. This research is accompanied by an open-source Python package called FitLand, which enables users to visualize the fitness landscape of their own models and provides a starting point for further research into the fitness landscape of deep learning. To accurately determine the characteristics of these events, the T2SHiNe and iDeep detectors require a precise understanding of how muons are detected in the context of their energy, direction, and whether the neutrino was initially muon or antimuon. To this end, a comprehensive study of the T2SHiNe and iDeep detectors' response to high-energy muon neutrino and antineutrino events was conducted using Monte Carlo simulations of the detectors and the neutrino interactions. This study explored various neutrino energies ranging from 5 GeV to 20 GeV and demonstrated that the detectors can efficiently identify muons produced by these interactions, even when the neutrinos are directed at the detectors at relatively shallow angles. Furthermore, the study found minimal distinction between muon and antimuon interactions in this energy range, allowing for the combination of these data in analyses. A statistical approach was employed to evaluate the detectors' ability to accurately determine the direction and energy of the initial neutrino, as well as whether it was a muon neutrino or antineutrino, based on the detected muon characteristics. This evaluation revealed that the detectors can determine the neutrino type with a confidence level above 0.9 for energies above 7 GeV, and can accurately calculate the initial neutrino energy and direction with a margin of error less than a factor of 2 for energies above 10 GeV. The study's findings will be valuable in reconstructing neutrino energies in the T2SHiNe and iDeep experiments and will also be applicable to other long baseline experiments that detect muons in the forward direction. The OT problem is notorious for its slow convergence rate when using first-order optimization methods, and although faster-order methods can solve this problem more efficiently, they typically require significant resources and are impractical for high-dimensional data sets.  In contrast, we present an approximate, dimension-reduced solution to the OT problem, based on a randomized OT subsampling method that produces a representative, lower-dimensional proxy to the original data.   uncertain, potentially leading to an exponentially expanding universe at the

instead of sign transformation. This transformation results in a symmetry that
is spontaneously broken, yielding a cosmologically stable dark sector made up
of non-gravitationally bound particles. This framework is compatible with both
high-energy particle collider experiments and cosmic microwave background data. 
It predicts a specific ratio for the dark matter to dark energy density, a
feature that can be verified through large-scale structure surveys and
gravitational wave observations of dark matter halos.

formation in an exponentially expanding universe, offering a unified explanation
for the composition of dark matter and dark energy.

particle accelerators and suggests that future detectors for dark matter made
out of light and extremely sensitive equipment may be compromised by the
presence of a large dark sector.

physics, and cosmological observations.

telescopes capable of detecting high-energy gamma radiation emitted from the

bound dark sector and provide a comprehensive explanation for the prevalence
of matter in the universe.

  challenge. In this paper, we introduce a large-scale, openly accessible 
  dataset called EmojiNet that systematically maps emojis to their semantic 
  equivalents in the form of WordNet concepts. The dataset comprises 335 
  classes of WordNet concepts and over 70,000 associated emojis, with over 
  30,000 distinct images. We demonstrate the efficacy of EmojiNet in several 
  tasks, including the classification of missing WordNet concepts for a given 
  emoji, the classification of emojis associated with a given WordNet concept, 
  and the training of a model to predict WordNet concepts for a given text 
  snippet containing emojis. Furthermore, we highlight potential applications 
  of the dataset in areas like sentiment analysis and machine translation.

  as a foundational resource for the integration of emojis into various NLP 
  frameworks. The dataset and code are available at https://emenet.org/.

However, the GD framework allows us to reframe this equivalence using only the specification, the GD system, and the desired output, effectively sidestepping the complexities of quantifiers and relations. By leveraging this improvement, we developed a method to validate the rounding modes according to IEEE754 standards using the Coq proof assistant. Consequently, we successfully applied this strategy to certify the floating-point implementations in the CompCert C compiler, the Clight compiler, and the fenv module in the Coq standard library. However, this replacement can lead to inaccuracies due to the loss of summation functionality. We propose a novel neural network framework that leverages a set theory-based generalization to ensure the correctness of these operations, guaranteeing that the modified network maintains the same mathematical properties as the original one. We emphasize that our findings are compatible with existing observational data on TeV BL Lac objects, and we anticipate that upcoming experiments with improved sensitivity will be able to confirm these predictions through more precise measurements of the polarization of these objects. Ultimately, we believe that confirming these predictions will significantly enhance our comprehension of relativistic jets and blazars. , high-speed data transmission is now a necessity, driving the development of ever-faster communication technologies.  In the pursuit of rapid data exchange, microwave communication systems are increasingly being integrated into vehicle networks, leading to rising concerns about the potential for communication signals to interfere with automotive radar systems, which rely on the same frequency band.  In this research, we examine the effects of microwave signals on a frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar system and investigate methods to mitigate this interference through modifications to the radar signal processing and antenna design.  Specifically, we analyze the spectral regrowth of the radar signal, which exacerbates interference, and propose a nonlinear signal processing technique called the exponential cumulative sum (ECS) method to rectify this issue.  Additionally, we explore the benefits of using an antenna with a notch in its frequency response to reduce interference and present simulation and experimental results to validate our approach.  Our findings demonstrate that with suitable signal processing and antenna design, the effects of microwave signals on the radar system can be minimized, paving the way for safe integration of communication systems into vehicle networks.  This research has implications for the coexistence of radar and communication systems across multiple frequency bands, including 5G and 6G networks. Therefore, this compound is highly promising for developing high-performance ferrimagnetic materials with strong electron-electron interactions. This study's findings can serve as a foundation for exploring the physics and potential applications of Co$_{20}$Ge$_{2}$ through advanced spectroscopic techniques and theoretical calculations. This analysis also reveals that these groups consist of inner automorphisms that can be represented by diagonal matrices, thereby providing a detailed understanding of the structure of these centralizers. To achieve this, we establish a connection between cocharacters of finite monomial groups and the Bruhat-Tits building, utilizing this framework to determine the image of these cocharacters on the vertices of the building. This, in turn, enables us to define groups of root operators that act on the cocharacters, resulting in the creation of a chain of commutative groups that reflects the nested structure of these image sets within the building. This chain, in turn, mirrors the structure of the groups themselves, thereby facilitating an examination of their geometric properties via this natural embedding within the building.   equipping it with a Wick ordering that maintains positivity, thus enabling the application 
  of semi-classical methods. Building on their work, this paper extends their theory to a 
  lattice of any dimension greater than two by introducing a new type of operator known 
  as a generalized time-ordering operator that is compatible with the lattice structure 
  and ensures the positivity of the Wick ordering. As a result, we can utilize the 
  semi-classical approximation to obtain reliable predictions for expectations of any 
  local operator in both the quantum and classical regimes. Furthermore, we establish 
  that the generalized time-ordering operator can be represented as a product of 
  commutators and anti-commutators of the lattice's creation and annihilation operators

  operator that includes both discrete and continuous terms, offering a comprehensive 
  framework for the analysis of the lattice's quantum behavior as it transitions to 
  the classical regime. As a specific example, we apply this approach to investigate 
  the lattice's quantum fluctuations surrounding a classical solution that represents 
  an oscillon in the $\phi^4$ theory, uncovering the lattice's quantum regime and 
  identifying the parameters that influence the oscillon's stability.

  modeled on lattices of any dimension greater than two with a finite volume,

  oscillon's stability.

  classical solution can be characterized by an exponential decay that is 
  controllable, invertible, and depends on the lattice's spacing, volume, and 
  energy cutoff, and on the dimensionality of the lattice.

  fluctuations surrounding a classical solution that represents an exponential decay

on Advanced Signal Processing for Healthcare Technologies and addresses the critical issue of reliable and accurate biometric sensing in wearable devices.  Biometric sensors in wearable devices are susceptible to signal corruption from various sources such as motion artifacts, electrical interference, and device malfunctions. As wearable devices have become ubiquitous, developing robust and reliable biometric sensing techniques is essential to ensure high-quality healthcare services.  This paper focuses on advanced signal processing methods to enhance the accuracy of biometric measurements in wearable devices.  Specifically, we explore cutting-edge techniques such as deep learning, sparse learning, and compressive sensing to address common issues in biometric sensing, including motion artifact removal, noise reduction, data compression, and classification improvement.  We examine the application of these techniques in widely used biometric sensors including ECG, EEG, and accelerometer sensors.  Finally, we outline promising research directions and potential challenges in this field. This study demonstrates the feasibility of creating a highly stable interface between two distinct oxide layers, MnOx and VOx, on a gold substrate using atomic layer deposition.  By varying the temperature and pressure during deposition, it is possible to control the orientation of the oxides and their interface through the formation of specific crystal phases, ultimately influencing the electrical and magnetic properties of the interface.  In particular, creating a specific phase of MnOx allows for the direct manipulation of the thin film's magnetic moment by adjusting the oxygen content, providing a means to precisely control the magnetic properties of transition-metal oxides through atomic layer deposition.  This research offers a new method for tailoring the physical properties of transition-metal oxides at the nanoscale by manipulating the crystal phases and their interfaces through precise control of chemical reactions.  This discovery paves the way for further investigation into the effects of atomic-scale defects and doping on the physical properties of transition-metal oxides, and demonstrates the potential of atomic layer deposition to control the magnetic, electrical, and optical properties of materials at the nanoscale.  This study's findings can be applied to develop precise control over the physical properties of oxides in field-effect transistors, and to engineer the properties of heterostructures with multiple interfaces and layers.  This research also provides insights into the fundamental physics of small-scale materials and their interfaces, and has implications for the development of high-performance memory devices, quantum computing, and advanced sensing technologies.  This study's results have been protected by a patent, and further research is being conducted to scale up the process to larger areas while maintaining precise control over the material's properties.   to being impacted by weather conditions such as fog, rain, and snow. Understanding
  the natural propagation patterns of these frequencies in various weather states is
  crucial for accurately modeling their behavior and ensuring reliable operation in
  real-world applications. This paper presents an analysis of the effects of weather
  conditions on the propagation of mmWave and terahertz frequencies through a
  theoretical examination of the scattering cross-sections of water and ice particles,
  followed by experimental validation using a sounding system in a controlled
  precipitation chamber. The results of this research demonstrate that the influence
  of weather conditions on the propagation of these frequencies is minimal, with
  scattering losses being significantly lower than the natural decay observed in
  natural environments. Consequently, the impact of particle scattering on signal
  attenuation in actual deployments is likely negligible, allowing for reliable
  operation in a wide range of weather conditions. Ultimately, the findings of this
  study can be applied to improve the accuracy of propagation models in weather

  electrons within reconnection fields, and suggests that the X-ray luminosity

of solutions to a system of partial differential equations describing viscous shock waves in a gas subject to non-entropy producing combustion, where the reaction rate is dependent on the density of the gas. This system of equations includes a nonlinear parabolic equation with a discontinuous, single-humped coercivity-inducing function, and includes the Barenblatt-Teng equation as a special case. We establish that viscous shock waves in this system satisfy the strong ray convexity property, which enables us to establish their uniqueness and establish that they are stable when the reaction rate is limited, similar to an upper bound. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of solutions to the full system of equations, including the reaction equation, in the super-solutions to the parabolic equation, which includes the case of initially compactly supported solutions. We establish that these solutions eventually become extinct in time and that there exists a universal constant that restricts the reaction rates. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the specific case of the Rayleigh-Taylor instability, where we derive a new nonlinear inequality that enables us to establish the existence and stability of solutions to a system of equations that includes a nonlinear fourth-order parabolic equation. We establish that these solutions satisfy the strong ray convexity property, which enables us to establish their uniqueness and establish that they are stable when the reaction rates are limited, similar to an upper bound, where this bound can be calculated explicitly. We believe that our work provides a significant contribution to the study of viscous shock waves in combustion and to the study of Rayleigh-Taylor instability in combustion and to the study of nonlinear fourth-order parabolic equations. These spaces can serve as substitutes in various mathematical proofs and applications, demonstrating the validity of the statement for metric spaces also holds in generalized metric spaces. This study investigates the fixed point theory in generalized metric spaces, presenting an alternative to the Banach fixed point principle that can be expressed as follows: if a generalized metric space is endowed with a distance function d, and for any points x and y in the space, the distance between x and y satisfies the condition d(f(x),f(y)) is less than or equal to max{d(x,y),d(x,y)/2,d(y,x)/2}, then f has a fixed point in the space. This generalized version of the Banach fixed point principle is then applied to demonstrate the existence of a fixed point for a function defined in a set of positive real numbers for which the distance between two points can be less than or equal to the maximum of the two numbers. This example illustrates that the strengthened version of the Banach fixed point principle is more powerful than its original version. This study also explores the concept of generalized metric spaces that satisfy the condition of 3/4 instead of the maximum of 1, 1/2, or 1/2, providing a straightforward proof for the fixed point existence in these spaces. This study aims to contribute to the ongoing exploration of generalized metric spaces by providing a strengthened version of the Banach fixed point principle and offering a comparison with existing versions. This study also highlights the need for further research on the applicability of the strengthened version of the Banach fixed point principle to various mathematical theories. Furthermore, our solution successfully found the action causing a counterexample in 100% of cases. We also applied our method to a real-world scenario with 5 mobile robots in a 10x10 meters space and obtained a satisfactory result. We believe our approach paves the way for applying supervisory control to complex robotic systems in real-world settings. To facilitate further development, we made our code available online. Results are expressed as customized three-particle correlation functions, known as $v_3$ coefficients, which are derived from the two-particle correlation function $v_2$ for charged particles. The investigation spans a range of transverse momentum (1 GeV to 20 GeV) and occurs in the central rapidity region. With increasing two-particle transverse momentum, $v_3$ coefficients exhibit a gradual decrease, and the study reveals a relationship between $v_3$ and mean transverse particle multiplicity, $M$, which can be described by the function $v_3 \propto M^{-0.5}$. The findings are consistent with existing data from lower energy proton-proton collisions and are also in agreement with theoretical predictions from quark gluon plasma turbulence and color glass condensate models. The study's limitations are discussed, and potential sources of $v_3$ variation, such as midrapidity particle multiplicity, should be explored in future experiments. The measured three-particle correlation function $v_3$ coefficients and their dependence on mean transverse particle multiplicity are now available for theoretical models to test and interpret. Building on this foundation, we conduct a series of multi-experiment trials with a varying format, where subjects participate in multiple experiments with different sets of spatial information. To understand the cognitive map each subject builds in each experiment, as well as the map they carry over from previous experiments, we use a computational model of spatial cognition. The outcomes of the multi-experiment trials are then compared to our model's predictions. The results show that the format of the initial experiment influences how subjects build their cognitive map, while the format of subsequent experiments has little effect. Furthermore, the information from the previous experiments is selectively forgotten by the subjects. We also observe that the format of the final experiment determines how the subjects' cognitive maps are combined, with the maps from previous experiments being either completely replaced or combined in a weighted average. We also investigate the concept of "cognitive map inertia" where subjects are resistant to changing their cognitive map in response to new information. We find that the degree of inertia varies based on the format of the previous experiment and the level of accuracy of the information provided in the new experiment. We conclude that the concept of cognitive map inertia is a critical factor in understanding how subjects navigate in virtual environments and that it is influenced by both their past and present experiences. We propose that the cognitive maps can be represented as a weighted Markov chain, where the weights reflect the resistance to change. We validate this representation by comparing our model's predictions with the actual outcomes of the multi-experiment trials. The comparison shows that the predicted outcomes accurately reflect the actual outcomes, as evidenced by the high degree of consistency between their respective distributions. We also examine the implications of this finding for the study of spatial cognition in virtual environments and the use of multi-experiment trials in psychology research. We propose that the format of the initial experiment should be designed to minimize the degree of inertia, while the format of the subsequent experiments should be designed to maximize the degree of change. We also suggest that the concept of cognitive map inertia can be generalized to other domains of study. We conclude that the study of spatial cognition in virtual environments through multi-experiment trials offers a promising approach for advancing our understanding of this phenomenon

  assess if the learned abilities are directly related to the dialogue provided
  during training. Our proposed approach addresses this limitation by introducing
  a new evaluation method that measures the effectiveness of learned abilities in
  areas outside of trained dialogue scenarios, which we call "out-of-dialogue"
  domains. In our experiments, we demonstrate that agents learning through
  interactive dialogue often suffer from a "Dialogue Overfitting" problem, where
  their abilities are more closely tied to the specific dialogue they were
  trained on rather than the underlying task. To address this issue, we propose
  a simple yet effective method called "Dialogue Pruning" that enhances the
  generalization of learned abilities in relation to the underlying task. Through
  our experiments, we show that Dialogue Pruning significantly boosts the
  performance of learned abilities in out-of-dialogue domains, providing a solid
  foundation for further research in this area. We also introduce a new dataset
  called "Dial2World" that facilitates the study of this problem, along with
  another dataset called "Dial2Out" that assesses the connection between
  trained dialogue scenarios and the underlying task in both in-dialogue and
  out-of-dialogue domains. Our proposed approach and datasets are available at
  https://github.com/google/dialog-overfitting. We hope this work sparks
  further research into the complex relationship between interactive dialogue and
  learning through experience. We also believe that our proposed method and
  datasets can be applied to other areas of research, such as the study of
  human learning through dialogue, as well as the development of more effective
  dialogue learning systems. We invite the research community to contribute to
  this area by sharing their own datasets and findings related to the "Dialogue
  Overfitting" problem. We also outline potential research directions for
  addressing this issue, including the development of more robust dialogue
  learning systems, as well as new evaluation methods for assessing the
  effectiveness of learned abilities in relation to the underlying task in both
  in-dialogue and out-of-dialogue domains. We believe that tackling this
  challenge will be crucial for the development of more reliable and efficient
  human-machine learning systems through interactive dialogue.

  physical aspects of fluid dynamics, with an emphasis on the Navier-Stokes
  equations and boundary layers. We delve into recent breakthroughs in understanding
  Navier-Stokes solutions, specifically the discovery that solutions within a
  boundary layer surrounding a rotating disk can be described using a specific
  mathematical structure. This structure, characterized by a unique set of
  invariant quantities, provides a framework for analyzing the behavior of these
  solutions and offers a compelling example of Prandtl's legacy in action. With
  this framework, we explore the features of solutions within the boundary layer
  and investigate its stability, revealing that solutions within the boundary
  layer surrounding a rotating disk behave in a complex, periodic manner as the
  spin speed increases. Furthermore, we propose a new hypothesis that these
  solutions within the boundary layer undergo a sudden, drastic change in
  behavior at a specific rotation speed, which aligns with experimental findings
  and offers a potential explanation for the onset of turbulence in rotating
  systems. Through the lens of Prandtl's boundary layer equation, we examine
  the dynamics of these systems and uncover the underlying mechanisms driving
  nonlinear, periodic behavior and eventually turbulence. To validate our
  hypothesis, we develop a new method for directly detecting the characteristic
  changes in the rotation number from numerical solutions of the Navier-Stokes
  equations, which we apply to a range of rotating systems, including a specific
  setup with a non-uniform wall and a rotating Taylor-Couette system with a
  free surface. By analyzing these systems, we uncover the complex, nonlinear
  dynamics of the primary bifurcation and the onset of the nonlinear, periodic
  behavior, as well as the eventual transition to the secondary, nonlinear
  behavior and the resulting turbulence. Through our study, we reveal the
  fundamental role of Prandtl's boundary layer equation in understanding the
  dynamics of rotating systems and the Navier-Stokes equations, particularly in
  the transition from laminar to turbulent flow. We also propose a new
  perspective on the concept of a critical layer and its relationship with the
  boundary layer and the underlying geometry of the system. We further explore
  the implications of our findings on the design of rotating systems, including
  those with a free surface, and discuss the potential applications of our
  research in fields such as astrophysics and fluid dynamics.

  the collapse of a molecular cloud core.  However, the process of how
  this star formation occurs is still not well understood.  Observations
  of the formation of massive stars are typically made after significant
  progress has been made, with the star already being quite massive
  and the cloud core being significantly depleted.  As a result, there
  is a lack of data on the early stages of massive cloud core collapse,
  particularly in regards to the presence of outflows.  To address
  this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive survey of massive
  cloud cores across the Milky Way using the APEX telescope to detect
  outflows and determine the level of dust polarization.  With this
  information, we were able to infer the orientation of magnetic fields
  and investigate their influence on the cloud core collapse.  Out of
  105 massive cloud cores surveyed, 63 were found to have outflows
  and 34 had detectable dust polarization, with magnetic fields
  found to play a significant role in the formation of massive stars
  in certain environments but not others.  Furthermore, we discovered
  that cloud cores with outflows, polarization, and magnetic fields
  are more likely to form massive stars than those without these
  features.  We also found that the presence of outflows in cloud cores
  is linked to the alignment of magnetic fields, suggesting that
  forces such as turbulence and gravity influence the alignment of
  magnetic fields in these environments.  With this new data, we
  re-examined existing models of magnetic field influence on cloud
  core collapse and found that they do not accurately reflect
  observations.  To address this discrepancy, we propose a new
  model in which magnetic fields influence the collapse of cloud cores
  by aligning with the axis of rotation, thus facilitating
  the formation of massive stars.  This model is supported by
  observations of cloud cores with outflows, polarization, and
  magnetic fields, and it provides a potential explanation
  for the formation of massive stars in molecular cloud cores.

We investigate how these systems change under various types of switchings, including additions, deletions and reconfigurations of their switching lines, at both the points of switching and in the system's attractor basin. Our findings show that while some switchings create bifurcations that result in the disappearance of attractors, others lead to the creation of attractors with non-linear structures, and can even cause the system to become non-switching with non-linear dynamics. Most notably, we discover that a specific type of switching, which we call the Pseudo-Border-Collision Bifurcation (PBCB), can lead to the creation of a strange attractor in a switchingly driven system with only one state variable. To confirm our results, we conducted numerical simulations to visualize these attractors and their associated dynamics. Moreover, we provide a PBCB-based mechanism that may explain the emergence of chaotic behaviour in a well-known non-smooth system. Finally, we highlight the significance of our research and its potential applications in understanding and managing the complex dynamics of switchingly driven systems. To better understand this dilemma, we have conducted an epidemiological study using a modified SEIR model, accounting for both the vaccine's protective effects against the virus's spread and the rare side effects of the vaccine. By analyzing the model's dynamics, we have identified key conditions under which the suspension of AstraZeneca's vaccine may lead to an increased risk of the pandemic's resurgence. Therefore, our findings suggest that in areas with severe pandemic outbreaks, the suspension of AstraZeneca's vaccine may ultimately exacerbate the problem it aims to solve, albeit through complex temporal dynamics. Consequently, policymakers should carefully weigh the potential benefits against the risks before implementing similar policies in the future. Ultimately, our research emphasizes the need for timely and accurate data on vaccine-related side effects and the transmission dynamics of the virus to inform informed policy decisions in this high-stakes situation. We examine expected stopping times to reach a boundary under the condition that the last $k$ coordinates sum to a certain value, revealing an expected stopping time for this event. By analyzing the probability of this sum via a convolution of discrete binomial distributions, we derive an expected stopping time expression. icksen-Liu mechanism for spontaneous solidification in liquid metals subjected to shock waves. Initially, the model was applied to a specific scenario where a solid layer forms beneath a superheated bulk liquid. However, we expand on this concept by incorporating the Ericksen-Liu mechanism into a model that includes a solid layer at the surface as well. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the formation of the surface solid layer can occur spontaneously, even in the absence of nucleation sites. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this surface solidification layer can become sufficiently thick to withstand the pressure of the shock wave, thereby preventing the formation of the lower solid layer in the bulk liquid. Consequently, this surface layer may mislead researchers, as it could conceal the true extent of the solidification process. In order to accurately assess the validity of the Ericksen-Liu mechanism in the surface scenario, we employed a different approach that directly accounts for the stress state in the liquid metal. By comparing the two models, we discovered that the surface solid layer formed through stress relaxation in the liquid metal results in a similar distribution of mass, albeit with a minor difference where the lower solid layer is thinner. This phenomenon is attributed to the increased pressure exerted on the upper solid layer by the overlying liquid metal, which accelerates the lower solid layer towards the shock front, thereby reducing its thickness. As a result, the surface solid layer's formation through the Ericksen-Liu mechanism in the surface scenario may be considered a minor process that does not significantly impact the overall mass distribution. Consequently, the surface solid layer that forms through stress relaxation in the liquid metal can be considered a manifestation of the Ericksen-Liu mechanism in the surface scenario. In order to validate our numerical results, we compared them with available experimental data on shock-induced solidification in liquid metals. By analyzing the X-ray radiography images, we were able to extract information about the mass distribution in the sample. Through this analysis, we found that the surface solid layer's thickness varied between 0.5 to 1.5 mm, which is consistent with our numerical predictions. Furthermore, we discovered that the lower solid layer's thickness decreased with an increase in the shock intensity, which is also supported by our numerical simulations. In conclusion, our numerical simulations accurately captured the complex process of shock-induced solidification in liquid metals, including the formation of surface solid layers through stress relaxation in the liquid metal. Consequently, this process can be described by the Ericksen-Liu mechanism in the surface scenario.

Instead, we assume that the conformal scalar curvature has a specific asymptotic behavior at the boundary. This achievement is made possible by our novel result showing that a sequence of conformally flat data, with a certain asymptotic behavior and a specific symmetry, can be made close to a known data set if and only if a particular asymptotic coefficient is non-zero. This fact becomes particularly significant when combined with the previous result of the first author, which together guarantees that a sequence of asymptotically flat data with vanishing traceless part can be approximated by a collection of data sets of a known type if and only if the sum of their corresponding asymptotic coefficients is non-negative. This outcome arises from the second variation formula of the conformal Helfer functional, established under the assumption of axisymmetry. using a deep learning framework, specifically a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), to identify the location of scintillation crystals within a calorimeter. We utilize a highly detailed and realistic simulation of the LHCb Scintillating Fibre Electromagnetic Calorimeter to train and test a CNN. The goal is to determine the position of scintillation crystals to precisely measure photon energies. A series of tests demonstrate that a CNN can accurately identify crystal positions even when the particles are Compton-scattered within the detector, and that it performs well in the presence of simulated trigger and read-out effects. A comparison of CNN performance to traditional tracking methods reveals a significant improvement in position resolution, leading to improved energy resolution for Compton events. Furthermore, the efficient and robust nature of the CNN makes it suitable for real-time particle identification in the LHCb experiment.   $G$ involve first determining a 2-edge connected spanning subgraph of $G$, as seen

Our achievement is made possible by implementing a refined version of the nonlinear maximum principle, originally developed by Chemin, Desjardins, and Grenier, along with a new energy inequality that incorporates a specific time-dependent factor, resulting in an improved stability estimate that surpasses the $B^{7/2}$ norm. For the sketch to remain effective, it must be updated in response to new road openings and blockages. However, the limited understanding of OAM mode behavior in the presence of real-world turbulence poses a significant challenge for practical implementation. This study investigates the effects of Kolmogorov turbulence on the propagation of light carrying OAM through free-space optical links. Analytical expressions are derived to describe the degradation of signal quality and mode scrambling in OAM carriers under Kolmogorov turbulence conditions. Furthermore, statistical simulations are conducted to model the behavior of OAM modes in real-time scenarios. The results of these simulations are then used to develop a mode-scrambling threshold, which indicates that the Kolmogorov turbulence needs to exceed a certain level to cause significant mode scrambling. The findings of this research can be applied to design robust OAM-based free-space optical communication systems by incorporating measures to mitigate Kolmogorov turbulence in the system's architecture. The developed mode-scrambling threshold can be used as a reference for future experimental validation. The proposed simulation framework can be expanded to study the effects of other types of turbulence on OAM modes. The derived analytical expressions can be applied to investigate the behavior of OAM modes in other scenarios, such as the combination of turbulence and atmospheric disturbance, and in single-mode fiber systems.   and ad-hoc networks, providing insights into its utility in these contexts.

  to gain a deeper understanding of delay-related performance in real-time systems 
  and to inform future research on routing protocols in wireless networks.

  various applications, emphasizing the metric's flexibility and practicality 
  in evaluating routing protocols in real-time systems.

By applying this privacy framework, we create a theoretical mechanism that maps source data to model parameters while maintaining privacy. for calculating the approximate Euclidean distance join (EDJ) in a distributed setting, where nodes represent points in a multi-dimensional space and want to find other points within a certain distance from them. We introduce a new protocol called '2H' that enables nodes to determine their approximate position in the join tree and exchange relevant data with neighboring nodes. The 2H protocol consists of two phases: an initial 'half' phase where nodes narrow down their possible connections to a specific range, followed by a 'double' phase where they expand their search to include more potential points. We prove the 2H protocol achieves optimal half and double phases in terms of message exchange for each point, leading to a total that adds up to our benchmark. Furthermore, we establish that the 2H protocol yields the lowest total message exchange among all known algorithms, surpassing our benchmark for specific dimensions like 4, 5, etc., and achieving a general dimension-specific formula for our benchmark, which we term the '2H cube', defined as the product of (d choose 2) multiplied by the sum of the first (d-1) positive integers, plus the search size d, plus 1. Notably, our results also apply to a variant of the 2H protocol where nodes are divided into levels and only the outermost levels exchange data. We believe the 2H protocol offers a valuable starting point for further research on efficient distributed algorithms for multi-dimensional data. We have implemented the 2H protocol in a Python program called 'distspy' that generates random node networks and calculates their message complexity using the 2H protocol, as well as a more advanced variant called 'distspy_double'. We also provide a companion website with the program's source code and additional details on the 2H protocol and its applications. We have tested the 2H protocol on large datasets for dimensions 3 and above and found that the best configuration for our benchmark involves a 'double' phase with a search size of 2^k-1, where k is the number of levels, and we recommend this configuration for general use. We have validated the 2H protocol's performance against a hypothetical optimal protocol for specific dimensions like 4, 5, etc., and found that it achieves nearly the minimum message exchange required to calculate the EDJ in those dimensions.   sensitivity to motion artifacts poses a significant challenge for their use.
  This issue is particularly pronounced in outdoor settings with varying
  illumination. To address this limitation, this research focuses on developing
  a novel method for removing motion artifacts from ToF images in real-time.
  Initially, the approach extracts the motion artifacts' characteristics by
  analyzing the inconsistencies in the ToF images' phase information across
  successive frames. This is achieved through a novel algorithm that utilizes a
  weighted average to combine the phase information from the current and
  preceding frames. The resulting value is then fed into a thresholding
  operation, which generates an indicator of the motion artifacts present in
  each pixel. This indicator is subsequently used in a weighted average
  operation to produce a phase information value that represents the ideal
  projection distance for each pixel. This value is then compared to the
  originally captured projection distance to determine the motion artifacts
  present in each pixel. This information is then used to calculate a
  confidence value for each pixel, which is then used in a weighted average
  operation to produce the final ToF image intensity values. This process is
  implemented using a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) to facilitate
  real-time processing. Experimental results show that this method effectively
  removes motion artifacts from ToF images in real-time, with minimal impact

  reduce motion artifacts by a factor of 3.5 in indoor settings and by a

Due to the dynamic nature of distribution systems, traditional methods that rely on static data are no longer effective in achieving coordinated and safe system operation.  This study presents a novel optimization model that accounts for the impact of voltage regulators on load flow and takes into consideration the influence of branch overloads on distribution lines.  This model enables the automatic coordination of protective relays, considering system configuration changes caused by voltage regulators and branch overloads during both normal and abnormal operating conditions.  A computational example using a real-world distribution system demonstrates the model's effectiveness in achieving coordinated and safe system operation.  Furthermore, this study highlights potential risks associated with the traditional coordination method based on static load flow and presents possible solutions to improve the accuracy of load flow calculation.  A discussion on the optimization model's limitations and potential extensions is also provided.  A computational case study using MATLAB and PSSE demonstrates the feasibility of this approach in actual system environments.  This research contributes valuable insights to distribution engineers on the selection and placement of voltage regulators and protective relays in distribution systems.   where the lattice points can be either 'open' or 'blocked'. At each step, 
  the walker chooses a neighboring site at random, with the outcome determined 
  by whether it's open or blocked. If an 'open' site is chosen, the walker

  the walker returns to the previous site and the site remains blocked.

  inverse survival function as a sum of exponential terms.

  as Dyck paths.

Perot cavity is a versatile tool for precision measurements in a variety of experiments, including atomic interferometry, but its sensitivity to motion is also a major source of error. To minimize this influence and improve the accuracy of atomic interferometry, researchers have developed a method to dampen the cavity's oscillations by injecting a specific type of light that counteracts motion-induced phase shifts. This technique, known as "phase-noise cancellation," has been shown to enhance the precision of atomic interferometry by reducing the impact of motion-induced noise. To further investigate this effect, researchers have modified the setup to measure the effect on atomic states directly. In this new measurement, they observed a reduction of over three orders of magnitude in the effect of motion on atomic states when using a cavity with a high-finesse filter, confirming that this technique is effective in reducing noise in precise measurements. To better understand this effect, researchers have developed a mathematical framework that describes how the cancellation mechanism reduces the influence of motion on atoms in a cavity. This framework reveals that the technique primarily reduces the effect of light scattering from atoms, rather than the influence of light on atoms, as previously thought. This new understanding of phase-noise cancellation could be useful in a variety of experiments, including atomic clocks and magnetometry, and has implications for optimizing these setups to minimize motion-induced error. To this end, researchers have identified an optimal configuration for a high-finesse filter that maximizes the effectiveness of phase-noise cancellation in a cavity. This optimal configuration is characterized by a specific relationship between the cavity's length and the distance between atoms, and is influenced by the frequency and polarization of the injected light. To further validate their findings, researchers have tested the effect of varying the frequency of the injected light and found that it has little impact on the effectiveness of phase-noise cancellation. This is because the frequency of the injected light is much lower than the frequency of the atomic transition, and as a result, the effect of light scattering from atoms is negligible. Although results on in-domain data have improved, evaluating the impact on far-out-of-domain data remains a pressing concern. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel two-stage approach to adapt BERT, which includes an initial stage focused on optimizing the model's representation space to enhance its general robustness, followed by a stage centered on fine-tuning the adapted model for a specific target domain. Through extensive experiments across both in-domain and far-out-of-domain settings, our approach consistently yields superior performance, demonstrating that domain adaptation can be beneficial even for distant data. To facilitate further research, we have made our adapted model and associated code publicly available.   images from online posts is a pressing issue. As a promising solution, neural 
  network optimization techniques have been applied to image removal tasks in 
  various contexts. However, the performance of these models has not been 
  previously evaluated using a dataset designed to assess the perceptual quality 
  of transformed images in real-world scenarios. In this research, a new test 
  set was created to measure the distortion introduced by optimized image 
  transformation models in both MNIST and CelebA-HQ face datasets. The results 
  showed that optimized models introduce noticeable quality degradation in low 
  resolution images and that the performance difference between them is 
  relatively small. Furthermore, a study was conducted to enhance the quality 
  of transformed images by fine-tuning the neural network that optimizes the 
  transformation function. The best approach identified was a simple one-step 
  process that yields superior results in the previously mentioned test sets. 
  This method's performance was found to be comparable to that of models designed 
  specifically for tasks such as image compression and style transfer. 
  Consequently, this research challenges the conventional wisdom that deep 
  neural network-based optimization techniques produce transformed images of 
  higher quality than shallow models. Moreover, the test sets developed in this 
  research are available for public use to facilitate further evaluation of 
  image transformation models in various applications.

The interconnection of AI systems creates complex, dynamic, and multi-layered relationships that can result in unpredictable effects when one system is compromised. However, this method requires a deep understanding of how light interacts with atoms and molecules in various energy states.  A crucial aspect of this understanding involves determining the most effective frequencies for photoassociation through the analysis of a specific phenomenon called two-photon transitions, where two photons are absorbed by a molecule to raise it to an excited atomic state.  This phenomenon can be both beneficial and misleading if not properly understood.  In this research, we investigate the relationship between two-photon transitions in photoassociation and present a method to identify them, distinguishing them from other processes that may result in similar effects.  We demonstrate this method's utility with data on the photoassociation of $^{87}$Rb$_2$ dimer in a specific vibrational state, where we found that two-photon transitions can lead to both missing and apparent frequencies.  This discovery highlights the importance of accounting for two-photon transitions when analyzing photoassociation spectra, specifically for molecules consisting of atoms with a large number of energy levels.  As a result, we recommend examining the spectral pattern resulting from the absorption of a single photon by an atom or molecule in a specific excited state, which we call the "spectral fingerprint".  This fingerprint can provide valuable insights into the physics governing two-photon transitions and help identify them, as seen in this research.  We also propose utilizing this information to guide theoretical models of photoassociation and coalescence processes.  Furthermore, we highlight the potential applications of two-photon transitions in controlled chemistry experiments, including the creation of molecules in specific excited states and the study of two-photon transitions in molecules consisting of different atoms.  As a result, we suggest that two-photon transitions should be considered both a challenge and an opportunity in controlled chemistry experiments.  We also emphasize the significance of accounting for two-photon transitions in experiments involving photoassociation, particularly when using specific frequencies to create molecules in certain vibrational states. Focusing on a two-dimensional square lattice with a specific orbital configuration, we investigate the phase diagram of these materials to understand how a particular type of nematic distortion affects their topological properties. Specifically, we examine how an anisotropic electric field affects the nematic phases and the resulting zero-energy Fermi arc states within the material's Weyl point. Our findings reveal that a unidirectional stress or an anisotropic electric field can induce nematic phases that either stabilize or destabilize the non-symmetric topological state, leading to a fragmentation of the phase diagram into multiple nematic domains. Furthermore, we propose feasible experimental signatures of these phases, including the zero-energy Fermi arc states and specific spectral features within the nematic domains. We propose that these materials could be investigated using techniques like angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and X-ray linear dichroism. We also suggest that material modifications, such as introducing point defects or changing the lattice periodicity, could be used to control the interplay between nematic and topological electronic phases. We conclude by emphasizing the importance of considering the interplay between nematic and topological phases in material design and the potential for studying these phases to reveal novel physics and experimental signatures. We outline the key parameters and Hamiltonians that govern these phases and propose that future theoretical and experimental studies could be guided by the established framework of this work. We also highlight the possibility of realizing robust zero-energy Fermi arc states and the need for experimental verification of the predicted magnetic order patterns and spectral features within the nematic domains. We propose that future studies could be directed towards understanding the interplay between nematic phases and other perturbations, such as spin-orbit coupling, electron-electron interactions, and lattice anharmonicity, as well as exploring the potential of these physics within other material classes and under different lattice geometries. on mobile devices in real-time 
  systems has become increasingly common, as they are now embedded in many 
  applications, including image and video processing, speech recognition, and 
  navigation. However, training large-scale ML models on mobile devices is 
  challenging due to their limited computational resources and memory. In contrast, 
  cloud-based infrastructure has ample computational power and storage capacity, 
  making it an ideal platform for training large-scale ML models. As a result, 
  there is a growing interest in outsourcing model training to the cloud while 
  keeping sensitive data private and secure on mobile devices. In this context, 
  Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising solution by enabling secure and 
  private model training across multiple devices without exchanging raw data. 
  Although FL addresses security and privacy concerns, it may still pose a threat 
  to data privacy if the ML model being shared is accessible to unauthorized 
  parties. In this paper, we introduce a new FL-based framework called Secure 
  Data-Free Federated Learning (SDFL), which protects data privacy by ensuring 
  the security of the shared ML model, in addition to protecting user data. 
  SDFL achieves this through a novel technique called model homomorphism, 
  ensuring that the shared model remains secure and private, even when used on 
  other datasets. In our experiments, SDFL demonstrates improved accuracy when 
  compared to existing FL-based frameworks that prioritize data privacy, and it 
  offers a seamless deployment experience for real-time applications on mobile 
  devices. We also provide a detailed analysis of the computational overhead 
  associated with SDFL, highlighting its efficiency on various mobile devices. 
  Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark called FedMAM, which assesses 
  FL-based applications through a combination of performance, energy efficiency, 
  and accuracy metrics. FedMAM facilitates the development of secure and 
  efficient FL-based applications on mobile devices, paving the way for real- 
  world deployments. In conclusion, SDFL presents a groundbreaking solution 
  for secure and private model training in real-time systems, offering a 
  versatile open-source codebase and a benchmark framework for the 
  research community to further refine and adapt it for various FL-based 
  applications. We anticipate that SDFL will inspire innovative solutions 
  for secure and private model training on mobile devices in real-time systems, 
  and we invite researchers to build upon our work by contributing to FedMAM

This level of detail allowed us to map the quasiparticle dynamics in the underdoped cuprate by reconstructing its energy, momentum, and temperature dependencies over a wide range. Our findings reveal that the normal state of YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.55}$ is characterized by a universal $T\chi(m,\pi)$ distribution that remains unchanged across temperatures from 60 K to 180 K, and a superconducting gap that increases with decreasing oxygen content. Furthermore, our measurements indicate that the spin excitations in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.55}$ have a momentum-dependent energy dispersion, a large orbital weight, and a temperature dependence that is in line with the activated Frohlich coherence factor suggested by theory. We also discovered that the weight of the $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave gap excitations decreases with increasing temperature above 150 K, and that this weight is directly correlated with the superconducting order parameter. Our research demonstrates that the complexity of underdoped cuprates stems from multiple competing interactions, and that the quasiparticle dynamics in these materials cannot be accurately described using either the Mott or the charge localization picture in isolation. Instead, both processes coexist and influence each other, leading to a variety of non-trivial outcomes that vary with temperature, oxygen content, and disorder. Our findings also highlight the significance of the $T\chi(m,\pi)$ distribution as a universal feature of the normal state of underdoped cuprates, and emphasize the need for further research into the origins of this distribution, as well as the $k$-dependent energy dispersion and the $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave gap excitations that characterize these materials. Our experiment's high-resolution, high-statistics data provide a comprehensive understanding of the normal and superconducting state of YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.55}$, and pave the way for a deeper comprehension of the competing interactions and quasiparticle dynamics in this material through theoretical modeling and numerical simulations. Our research also highlights the potential of high-energy resolution inelastic neutron scattering for studying the quasiparticle dynamics in other materials and the importance of considering the interplay between competing interactions in the study of strongly correlated electron systems. Networks in image recognition, using them for face identification in videos has become a popular alternative to traditional methods based on templates and biometrics.  However, as DNNs have grown in size and precision, they've developed vulnerabilities to manipulation through video editing, posing a significant threat to secure facial identification systems.  In this research, a new attack called Face2Face-ResNet50 was created that can easily generate high-fidelity, manipulated videos containing a specific individual's face, even with high-resolution cameras commonly used in public environments.  The innovative aspect of this attack is its ability to deceive a state-of-the-art facial recognition system based on DNNs, specifically based on ResNet50, in over 80\% of outdoor video footage shot at a medium distance.  The minimal time and computational resources required to produce this type of video make it a highly effective tool for compromising secure facial recognition systems in real-world settings.  The simple design of the Face2Face-ResNet50 algorithm allows for easy modification to create more complex manipulations, such as deepfake faces, and the research highlights the critical need for developing more secure facial recognition systems that can withstand such sophisticated video editing techniques. These systems often involve multiple sources that share information to determine optimal data collection routes, yet they typically operate independently without mutual knowledge. From the perspective of an outsider observer, these systems appear as interconnected, multi-hierarchical games where players at each source have independent knowledge, players at intermediate nodes make independent decisions and players at the collector have perfect knowledge. Our research focuses on studying the behavior of these systems to understand how they converge to their equilibrium state and to identify conditions that guarantee the convergence of their Nash equilibria to socially optimal solutions. Our results include designing a learning algorithm for source nodes, proving the convergence of hierarchical games to their Nash equilibria and demonstrating the convergence of these equilibria to optimal solutions under certain conditions. Our findings are validated through extensive simulations and provide insights into the parameters that influence the convergence of distributed data collection systems. With the aim of making these systems more efficient, we explore potential extensions to our work. In this research, we employed the Linear Enhanced Sequential Cumulative Improved Monte Carlo simulation tool to investigate the QCD hard and soft partonic flow effects on dilepton production in proton-probon collisions at the LHC energy. A newly developed soft QCD model, the "4PI improved" Fierz-Weiss-Venezo algorithm, was utilized to simulate QCD little by little. To better understand these results, we also examined the four-particle correlations in the light-cone momentum variable $x$. Our research demonstrates that the QCD hard and soft partonic flow effects on dilepton production can be quantified through the flow index $\gamma$ in relation to the average $x$ power, providing a unified framework for analyzing flow effects on various probes in QCD.   sentence similarity and classification models is a pressing concern. Research to
  date has primarily focused on highlighting the benefits of multilingual models,
  without delving into the potential drawbacks of training on multiple languages.
  We present an innovative approach to pinpointing the source of this
  generalization improvement by leveraging a computational framework that allows
  us to isolate and analyze the impact of each language within a multilingual
  dataset. Through a systematic analysis, we discovered that the primary boost
  in performance stems not from the additional languages, but rather from the
  larger dataset size resulting from the multilingual training data. This is
  supported by our findings showing that the optimal learning rate increases
  significantly with the size of the model, leading to all existing language
  data being effectively learned and contributing to improved performance.  In
  contrast, training on multiple languages without a common language ID yields
  subpar results.  Furthermore, we discovered that the optimal learning rate
  scales with the square root of the model size, providing a theoretical basis
  for the observed performance boost.  As a result, we propose a simple yet
  effective approach, dubbed BigZero, which achieves comparable performance to
  multilingual models by training on larger monolingual datasets, without the
  drawbacks associated with training on multiple languages.  Through extensive
  evaluations, BigZero has been shown to excel across 9 languages and 7
  NLP tasks, outperforming multilingual models in 50% of the cases studied.  In
  particular, BigZero yields a significant improvement of 4-6 points in the F1
  score on 5 out of 7 classification tasks, and 0.5-1.5 points in the Matthews
  beta score on 4 out of 7 relation extraction tasks.  We believe that our
  findings and approach can serve as a foundation for further research into
  efficient large-scale NLP training.  We have made our code and data available
  at https://github.com/parthaT2/bigzero.  We hope that our work inspires
  other researchers to explore the potential of large-scale NLP training.  We
  also outline potential avenues for future research, including investigating
  the optimal way to select and combine multiple monolingual datasets, as
  well as analyzing the underlying reasons for the observed performance boost
  associated with large-scale NLP training.
